title: Shabbat afternoon
hookLine: rest, a nap, a walk, study and friends; the Talmud calls Shabbat one sixtieth of the world to come (Berakhot 57b)

lines: A BOOK OPEN ON SOMEONE'S CHEST.
cards: Saturday, about two in the afternoon. Lunch was long. The dishes can wait.
Somebody's asleep on the couch with a book open on their chest. The kids are out in the yard, or at a friend's house down the street. Two neighbors walk slowly, going nowhere in particular.
Someone's reading. Nowhere to drive to, nothing to buy, no screen to check. If you've never had an afternoon like this, it can sound boring.
Some who have one every week say it's the part of the week they'd give up last.

teach.b: Menuchah means rest, but a full, settled kind of rest, not just collapse. There's a well-known teaching about Genesis.
It says God finished the work on the seventh day, and the rabbis asked: what was still missing, that was finished on the seventh day?
Rest. The world had everything, except menuchah. Came Shabbat, came rest.
Rest isn't the absence of creation. It's the last thing created.
The prophet Isaiah gave Shabbat a name people still use, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "call the sabbath a delight." Oneg, delight. So Shabbat afternoon is for delight.
A nap, which some people half joke is a religious duty. A slow walk. Friends dropping by.
Games with the kids. And study: in some communities, on summer Shabbat afternoons, people read Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a chapter a week.
Then there's the Talmud's list of things that are one sixtieth of something greater. Fire is one sixtieth of Gehinnom, the place of punishment. Honey is one sixtieth of manna.
Sleep is one sixtieth of death. A dream is one sixtieth of prophecy.

teach.h: ONE SIXTIETH OF THE WORLD TO COME.
teach.b: And Shabbat is one sixtieth of the world to come. A small taste. A sample.
The rabbis weren't describing the afternoon as a holiday from life, but as a preview of what life is ultimately for.
Whatever you believe about what's coming, the afternoon asks something simple: stop long enough to taste something, and see if it's good.

how: Shabbat afternoon is often spent after a long lunch napping, walking, visiting friends, playing with children and studying; some communities read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on summer Shabbat afternoons.

o: a short break between two work shifts
full, settled rest, the last thing created
sleep you take because you're worn out

games.q: what's inside the afternoon — tap the pairs.
p: a taste of the world to come

s: the rabbis said the world lacked only rest
on the seventh day, rest came into the world.
the Talmud calls Shabbat half of the world to come
it says one sixtieth: a taste, a sample.
Isaiah calls the Sabbath a delight
"call the sabbath a delight": oneg Shabbat.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis reading Genesis. God finished the work on the seventh day. but wasn't everything already made? what was still missing?
games.why: rest: the world had everything except menuchah. came Shabbat, came rest.

practice: Feel how heavy your body is in the chair, and let your shoulders drop a little lower.

Picture a stretch of time this week with nothing in it, and choose: a nap, eyes closed, phone in another room, or a walk with no destination and no podcast. Picture yourself doing it slowly, and let yourself look forward to it.

wordCard.voice: Menuchah. Settled rest, the last thing created, and on Shabbat afternoon a taste, the Talmud says, of the world to come.

orig.note: Hebrew: rest, calm. the same root as Noah, whose name is linked to comfort and rest.

carryVoice: Your line: a taste of what's coming. Oneg: call it a delight. Day one hundred six.

sources.ref: Rashi on Genesis 2:2; Genesis Rabbah 10:9 (rest was created)
